title: Anthropic IPO Explained: Price Range, Nasdaq Date, Google and Nvidia's $10 Billion Bets
subtitle: Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq as ANT around November 19. Here are the numbers, the $26 billion private placement, the risks, and the dates every investor should know.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: An IPO of this size is not just a financing event. It is a public vote on whether the AI boom has years of runway left or is running low on fuel.
The best IPOs are not judged on their first day. They are judged on the first four quarters.
Most investors in the deal are also suppliers, which raises fair questions about circular demand in AI.
excerpt: Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq as ANT around November 19, with Google and Nvidia each committing about $10 billion. We break down the numbers, risks and key dates.
content:
IPO Watch 2026

The most talked-about stock market debut of the year is days away. According to filings and news reports, Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude assistant, plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT around November 19, 2026, with a price range of $70 to $78 a share. Alongside the public offering, a group of seven strategic investors, led by Google and Nvidia at about $10 billion each, has agreed to buy a further $26 billion of non-voting stock at the IPO price. The listing arrives in the same week that Nvidia lost its CEO, which has turned an already closely watched deal into a stress test for the entire AI trade. This guide explains the numbers, the structure, the risks and the dates to watch.

What Is Happening: The Anthropic IPO in Plain English

An initial public offering, or IPO, is the moment a private company sells shares to the public for the first time. For founders and early backers, it is a chance to turn paper wealth into real money. For the company, it is a way to raise a large pool of capital. For ordinary investors, it is a first opportunity to own a piece of a business that was previously open only to venture funds and large institutions.

Anthropic filed an amended registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on or around November 10, 2026. Reports based on that filing put the expected price range at $70 to $78 per share, and Fortune reported that the company is expected to list on a Wednesday or Thursday this coming week. Several outlets are pointing to November 19 as the likely first trading day, though the final date and price depend on market conditions and the pricing process, so treat both as expectations rather than guarantees.

One analysis put the implied value at roughly $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion on a fully diluted basis. If those figures hold, Anthropic would debut among the most valuable companies in the world on day one, which is exactly why the deal is being compared to the biggest listings in market history.

“ An IPO of this size is not just a financing event. It is a public vote on whether the AI boom has years of runway left or is running low on fuel. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

The $26 Billion Private Placement Explained

The most unusual part of the structure is a private placement that runs alongside the public offering. According to the amended filing as reported by several financial outlets, seven companies have agreed to buy a combined $26 billion of Anthropic's non-voting Class N shares at the final IPO price, with the purchases settling immediately after the listing.

  • Google (Alphabet): about $10 billion, using an existing option in its 2026 financing agreement.
  • Nvidia: about $10 billion.
  • AMD: about $2.5 billion.
  • Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft: about $1 billion each.
  • TSMC: about $500 million.

Combined with the public offering, reports estimate the total raise could land between roughly $84.6 billion and $93.7 billion, depending on the final price and on whether underwriters use their option to buy additional shares. If that range holds, it would set a new record for money raised in a single listing. Non-voting shares are a notable detail: they give these partners a financial stake without giving them a say in how the company is governed.

Why Chipmakers and Cloud Giants Are Buying In

Look at the investor list and a pattern appears. Nearly every name is a supplier. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom design the chips used to train and run AI models. TSMC manufactures many of them. Micron supplies memory. Google provides custom TPU chips and cloud capacity. Microsoft sells cloud services. Reports say Anthropic has signed compute and infrastructure commitments exceeding $900 billion over the next decade, largely with these same kinds of partners.

From the suppliers' point of view, the logic is straightforward. A well-funded customer keeps buying chips and cloud time, and an equity stake lets them share in the upside if that customer grows. From a skeptic's point of view, it raises a fair question about circularity: when a company's biggest suppliers are also its biggest investors, how much of the growth is independent demand and how much is money moving in a loop? That debate has followed the entire AI sector this year, and the Anthropic listing will put it in front of public investors for the first time.

The Business Behind the Valuation

A valuation in the trillions needs a growth story to match, and the reported figures are striking. According to coverage of the filing, Anthropic's revenue for the first nine months of 2026 was about $33.2 billion, compared with roughly $2.5 billion in the same period a year earlier, while its operating loss narrowed from about $5.2 billion to about $1.3 billion. One report also cited a run-rate revenue of around $81 billion as of October 31, 2026. Run-rate figures annualize recent results, so they are a snapshot of momentum and not audited annual revenue.

Those numbers should be read with care. Growth this fast is unusual, and it leaves little room for disappointment. Public markets reward acceleration and punish slowdowns harshly. The company will also face new obligations as a listed business: quarterly earnings, detailed risk disclosures and constant scrutiny of how much it spends on computing power.

The Nvidia Factor: Why Timing Matters

The timing is awkward. On November 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned, naming CFO Colette Kress as interim chief executive. Nvidia is both Anthropic's key chip supplier and one of its anchor investors, and it reports its own quarterly earnings on November 17, just days before the expected listing. Fortune described the IPO as having become harder in the wake of the news, and noted that the earnings call will be Nvidia's first without Huang at the helm.

Investors quoted in coverage said Anthropic's underlying business is intact, but that the wider AI story is under new strain. One commentator observed that Nvidia's commitment to the offering will likely still go ahead, while expectations that Nvidia would act as an open-ended financial backstop for others in the ecosystem may cool. Nothing in the reporting suggests the deal is cancelled or delayed, and the timeline described in coverage remains unchanged as of this writing.

“ The best IPOs are not judged on their first day. They are judged on the first four quarters. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

What It Could Mean for Everyday Investors

Most retail investors will not be able to buy shares at the IPO price, because allocations at that level usually go to institutions first. The more practical question is how the listing touches portfolios people already own. Several analyses point out that big technology companies and broad index funds already hold indirect exposure to Anthropic through earlier investments and partnerships, so the debut could ripple through familiar names.

One analysis also noted that, if the stock debuts on November 19, index providers' rules could make a December inclusion in major indexes possible, which would force index funds to buy. That is a mechanical effect and not a guarantee, and it depends on each index's specific rules. As always, first-day pops and later declines are both common with large IPOs, and no one can reliably predict which will happen. This article is for information only and is not investment advice.

Risks and Questions Every Reader Should Know

  • Valuation risk. A price in the trillions assumes extremely strong growth continues for years.
  • Concentration risk. Heavy spending commitments to a few chip and cloud suppliers can strain margins if growth slows.
  • Circularity concerns. Suppliers who are also shareholders can make demand harder to read.
  • Governance structure. Non-voting shares for strategic buyers and ownership caps shape who controls the company.
  • Market conditions. A weak week for tech stocks, including fallout from Nvidia's leadership change, can affect pricing and early trading.
  • Competition. Rivals including OpenAI and Google are also racing for talent, customers and computing capacity.

Key Dates to Watch

The calendar is tight. Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, November 17. Pricing is expected around November 18, with trading expected to begin around November 19. After that, a seventh-trading-day reference date near the end of November could matter for index decisions, with possible index changes in late December. Dates in this kind of process can shift, so check the company's official filings and your broker for confirmed details.

The Bigger Picture for Business Leaders

Whatever happens on day one, the deal tells a bigger story. Capital is flowing into AI at a scale that few industries have ever seen, and the biggest companies in the world are using their balance sheets to lock in relationships with the leading model builders. For business leaders outside tech, the lesson is practical: the AI tools they rely on are being built by companies whose financing, customers and suppliers are tightly intertwined, so vendor strategy and contingency planning matter more than ever.

For employees and founders, the IPO is also a signal about talent. A public listing of this size creates liquidity for early staff and investors, and that often triggers a new wave of start-ups as people leave to build their own ventures. For the market as a whole, it is a rare moment when a single event can shift sentiment about an entire sector.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Anthropic IPO?

Reports expect Anthropic to price around November 18 and begin trading on Nasdaq around November 19, 2026. The final date depends on market conditions and the offering process.

What is Anthropic's stock ticker?

Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, according to financial coverage of the filing.

What is the Anthropic IPO price range?

The reported range is $70 to $78 per share. The final price is set just before trading begins and can differ from the range.

Who is investing $10 billion in the Anthropic IPO?

Google (Alphabet) and Nvidia have each agreed to buy about $10 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price, as part of a $26 billion private placement that also includes AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC.

Does Jensen Huang's resignation affect the Anthropic IPO?

Coverage describes added pressure and uncertainty, but no delay or cancellation had been reported at the time of writing. Nvidia's commitment is expected to proceed.

Can I buy Anthropic stock at the IPO price?

Most IPO allocations go to institutional investors. Individual investors can usually buy once shares begin trading, through a brokerage account, at the market price.

Key Takeaways • Anthropic IPO

Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq as ANT around November 19, with a reported range of $70 to $78 a share.

A $26 billion private placement from seven partners, led by Google and Nvidia at $10 billion each, runs alongside the offering.

Most investors are also suppliers, which raises questions about circular demand in AI.

Nvidia's CEO change and its November 17 earnings add pressure right before the debut.

The best IPOs are judged on the first four quarters, not the first day.

Bottom Line: “A giant listing, a nervous market, and a verdict on the AI boom.”

title: Why the Dow Jumped 1,500 Points After the 2026 Midterms: Winners, Risks and What CEOs Should Do
subtitle: The Dow had its best day since April 2025 after Democrats won Congress. Here is which sectors surged, what analysts say, and what business leaders should watch.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: Markets rarely vote for a party. They vote for clarity, and a clear result, whichever way it points, often feels like relief.
A one-day rally is a headline. A durable trend needs earnings, interest rates and policy to line up behind it.
A divided government usually means fewer sweeping laws and more oversight.
excerpt: The Dow closed up more than 1,500 points on November 4, 2026, its best day since April 2025. We explain the winners, the risks and what executives should watch.
content:
Markets & Politics 2026

When the midterm votes were counted, Wall Street did not wait for the commentary. On Wednesday, November 4, 2026, the day after Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up more than 1,500 points, its best day since April 2025. Oil prices fell, retailers, hospital operators and clean-energy companies jumped, and chief executives across industries began asking the same question: what does a divided Washington mean for business? This guide explains what happened, which sectors moved and why, what analysts say, and what executives should watch before the end of the year. It covers markets and economics only, and it does not take a political side.

What Happened to the Markets After the Midterms

The numbers were large. According to reports from the Associated Press and Reuters, the Dow closed up 1,569.40 points, or about 3 percent, at 53,356.12. The S&P 500 rose 119.70 points, or about 1.6 percent, to 7,688.62, which was its best day in three months. The Nasdaq composite gained 364.50 points to 25,736.51. The Dow's gain was its biggest single-day advance since April 9, 2025.

The move began in futures trading overnight as results came in. Earlier in the session, the Dow was up by roughly 1,300 points, and the rally held into the close. Reports noted that several results came in Republican strongholds, including wins by Democratic Senate candidates in states such as South Carolina and Texas, and Reuters reported that Democrats won seats in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations, which added to the sense that the result was decisive.

One useful piece of context from AP is that stocks generally tend to do well in the months after any midterm election, regardless of which party wins. In other words, part of the rally may reflect the removal of uncertainty and not a verdict on any particular policy.

“ Markets rarely vote for a party. They vote for clarity, and a clear result, whichever way it points, often feels like relief. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

Why Wall Street Cheered a Divided Washington

Analysts offered several explanations, and they are worth separating. The first is the idea of shared power. Dan North, a senior economist at Allianz Trade, said markets tend to like it when control of Congress and the White House is split between the parties, because major changes in either direction become harder to pass. A split government can be read as a brake on extreme policy swings, which investors often prefer.

The second explanation is the cost of living. Reports described rising prices as a top concern for voters, and some investors expected a new Congress to push policies aimed at easing household budgets, which could help retailers and consumer-facing companies. The third is energy. Oil prices fell sharply after the election, and the combination of lower fuel costs and hopes for consumer relief helped lift consumer discretionary stocks, the best-performing sector on the day.

None of these explanations is certain, and they can overlap. Markets move on expectations, and expectations can change quickly when new information arrives.

The Winners: Sectors That Led the Rally

The gains were not evenly spread. Reports highlighted several groups.

  • Consumer discretionary. This was the leading sector, with Amazon up about 7 percent, according to market reports.
  • Big technology. Alphabet rose more than 4 percent, and the Nasdaq gained alongside the broader market.
  • Clean energy. Solar and wind companies were early winners on hopes that a Democratic Congress could restore or expand federal support. AP reported that First Solar jumped nearly 10 percent and Enphase Energy more than 10 percent during the session.
  • Healthcare providers. Hospital owners were among the leaders, with analysts pointing to expectations that Democrats could try to reverse some past cuts to federal healthcare funding.
  • Discount retailers. Dollar stores serving lower-income shoppers rose on hopes for cost-of-living relief.

The Question Marks: Where Risks Remain

Not every sector celebrated. Analysts noted that Democratic control of the Senate in particular could create hurdles for artificial intelligence and technology legislation. Analyst Dan Ives said there is no way to sugarcoat that this would complicate the policy path for AI and tech companies. That matters because AI spending has been one of the biggest drivers of stock market gains over the past two years.

Falling oil prices also cut both ways. Lower fuel costs help consumers and airlines, but they usually weigh on energy producers, and they can reduce the financial incentive to switch to renewable power. Analysts said the clean-energy rally reflected the political outlook more than the oil price.

There is also the practical limit on what a new Congress can do. In an NPR discussion of the economic impact, correspondent Scott Horsley said that in the short run the result may not mean much for household budgets. Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, noted that Congress does not necessarily have the power to bring costs down on its own. A Democratic Congress could try to reassert its role on trade policy and the war in Iran, but the president keeps the veto pen, so major changes would need to survive that hurdle.

“ A one-day rally is a headline. A durable trend needs earnings, interest rates and policy to line up behind it. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

What This Means for CEOs and Business Leaders

For executives, the election changes the planning environment even if it does not change the economy overnight. Several themes stand out in analyst commentary.

  • Trade and tariffs. A Congress controlled by a different party from the White House may seek more oversight of trade policy, which matters for importers, manufacturers and retailers building next year's budgets.
  • Technology regulation. Companies in AI, data and platforms may face more committee hearings, bills and investigations, so government affairs teams will have more work to do.
  • Energy planning. Utilities, solar developers and energy-intensive manufacturers will watch for any change in federal incentives and permitting.
  • Healthcare funding. Hospitals, insurers and device makers will follow how Congress handles federal health programs and budgets.
  • Consumer demand. Retailers will watch for any policies aimed at living costs, along with fuel prices and employment data.

What History Says About Stocks After Midterms

Historians of market behavior often point out that the period after a midterm election tends to be positive for stocks. A common explanation is that the political calendar has become clearer: the big campaign promises are behind investors, and the president and Congress must work out a way to govern with the numbers they have. AP made the same point in its coverage, noting that the pattern holds regardless of which party wins.

History is a guide, not a promise. Every cycle has its own conditions, and this one includes high energy prices earlier in the year, stubborn costs for households and a heavy dependence of the stock market on a small group of AI-linked companies. A rally that begins on election week can fade if earnings disappoint or if inflation or interest rates surprise to the upside.

Other Forces Moving Markets This Month

The election is not the only story. In the days after the vote, Nvidia announced the resignation of its CEO, which shook the technology sector, and Anthropic prepared to go public in one of the largest IPOs ever attempted. Earnings season continued, with companies such as AMD reporting stronger profits than analysts expected. Energy prices remained a key swing factor for inflation and consumer spending. These crosscurrents are a reminder that a single day's gain should not be read as a forecast for the year.

What to Watch Between Now and Year-End

  • Transition signals. How the new Congress organizes itself, which committees it prioritizes and what its leaders say about trade, energy and technology.
  • Oil prices. Whether the post-election drop in crude holds, since fuel costs feed into inflation and consumer confidence.
  • Federal Reserve policy. Any signals on interest rates, which affect valuations more than most political news.
  • Corporate earnings and guidance. Whether companies raise or cut outlooks for 2027.
  • Technology policy. Early moves on AI, data privacy and antitrust issues.
  • Market breadth. Whether gains broaden beyond a few large technology names.

The Bigger Picture

The post-midterm rally is a reminder of how deeply politics and markets are connected, and how often the connection is misunderstood. A big green day does not mean investors prefer one party, and a bad day does not mean they reject another. More often, they are repricing risk: how likely is it that policy changes, how large would those changes be, and which companies are most exposed?

For business leaders, the practical takeaway is to plan for several scenarios instead of one. A divided government usually means fewer sweeping laws and more oversight, more negotiation and more uncertainty about deadlines. Companies that build flexibility into budgets, supply chains and hiring plans are better placed than those that bet on a single political outcome. This article is for information only and is not investment advice or political commentary.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did the Dow rise after the 2026 midterm elections?

The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,569.40 points, about 3 percent, on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, finishing at 53,356.12 according to AP and other reports.

Why did the stock market rally after the midterms?

Analysts pointed to relief that the uncertainty was over, the market's historical preference for divided government, falling oil prices and hopes for policies that ease living costs. Stocks also tend to do well in the months after midterms generally.

Which stocks and sectors gained the most?

Consumer discretionary stocks led, with Amazon up about 7 percent and Alphabet up more than 4 percent. Solar companies, hospital operators and discount retailers also posted strong gains.

What does a Democratic Congress mean for tech and AI companies?

Some analysts expect more scrutiny and a harder path for tech and AI legislation, particularly with Senate control changing hands, though the president retains veto power over new laws.

Does a stock market rally mean the economy will improve?

Not necessarily. Economists quoted in coverage said the short-term effect on household costs may be limited, and a one-day rally does not guarantee a lasting trend.

Is this article financial or political advice?

No. It summarizes reported market moves and analyst views for information only and does not recommend any investment or political position.

Key Takeaways • Markets After the Midterms

The Dow closed up 1,569 points, about 3 percent, on November 4, 2026, its best day since April 2025.

Consumer, clean-energy, healthcare and retail stocks led, while analysts flagged tougher road ahead for tech legislation.

Stocks tend to do well after midterms generally, so part of the move may be relief, not a policy verdict.

A divided government usually means more oversight and fewer sweeping changes, and the president keeps the veto.

title: John Ternus Is Apple's New CEO: What Changes After Tim Cook and What to Watch
subtitle: John Ternus replaced Tim Cook as Apple CEO on September 1, 2026. Here is who he is, what Cook does now, the challenges ahead, and the Nvidia twist.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: The hardest part of any succession is not choosing the next leader. It is letting the old one step back without letting the company wobble.
Apple does not need to win the AI race by building the biggest brain. It needs to put the best one in your pocket.
Investors reward predictability, and a planned handover is the best form of it.
excerpt: John Ternus became Apple's CEO on September 1, 2026, with Tim Cook as executive chairman. We explain who Ternus is, what changes and what to watch.
content:
Leadership Spotlight 2026

After fifteen years, the most famous handover in corporate America has happened. On September 1, 2026, John Ternus, the hardware engineer who helped create the iPad, AirPods and Apple Watch, became CEO of Apple. Tim Cook, who took over from Steve Jobs in 2011 and turned Apple into a multi-trillion-dollar giant, moved to the role of executive chairman. Weeks later, Cook's name surfaced again when President Trump suggested him as the next CEO of Nvidia. Here is a complete, plain-English guide to the Ternus era: who he is, what changes at Apple, what stays the same, and what to watch next.

The Handover: What Happened and When

Apple announced the transition in April 2026, after unanimous approval from its board. Cook said at the time that it had been the greatest privilege of his life to lead the company, and described Ternus as a visionary and the right person to lead Apple into the future. Ternus joined the board of directors when he became CEO, and Cook stayed on as executive chairman.

The timing was deliberate. Cook remained CEO through the summer while working with Ternus on the handover, and on the company's July earnings call Cook called his successor one of a kind and said the transition would go seamlessly. The long runway was designed to avoid the kind of market shock that surprise CEO changes can cause. A Fast Company report on the transition noted that Apple tested and tightly controlled how the news would be released, because leadership changes can send stocks tumbling.

Ternus's first major public moments as CEO were expected to come quickly, including Apple's September 9 hardware event, where the company was widely expected to unveil new iPhones and possibly its first foldable device.

“ The hardest part of any succession is not choosing the next leader. It is letting the old one step back without letting the company wobble. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

Who Is John Ternus?

Ternus joined Apple in 2001 and spent his career in hardware engineering, eventually becoming senior vice president of hardware engineering. In that role he oversaw the development of many of Apple's best-known products, including the iPad, AirPods, Apple Watch and the Vision Pro headset. He also became the familiar face of product launches, presenting Apple's hardware at major events such as WWDC.

He worked under Steve Jobs and has described Cook as his mentor. In his statement after the announcement, he said that having spent almost his entire career at Apple, he felt lucky to have worked under Jobs and to have had Cook as a mentor. Commentators often note that his rise had been anticipated for years. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman had reported that Ternus was the obvious successor, citing his technical depth, his rising public profile and the fact that he is roughly the same age Cook was when he took the top job.

His appointment marks the return of a chief executive with a product and design background, something Apple's last long-serving product-minded chief, Steve Jobs, also had. Cook came from operations and supply chain, which is why his tenure is remembered for efficiency, scale and services growth. Ternus comes from the engineering side, which suggests a different emphasis.

The Cook Era by the Numbers

To understand what Ternus inherits, look at what Cook built. According to coverage of the handover, Cook took the baton from Jobs in 2011 when Apple was worth roughly $350 billion and led it to a market value of around $4.5 trillion. Apple's shares rose more than 2,200 percent under his leadership, and annual sales grew from $108 billion to about $416 billion in the most recent fiscal year, according to one report.

Cook's success was built on a few pillars: an enormously efficient global supply chain, a growing services business including the App Store, iCloud and Apple Music, and a steady expansion of the product line from iPhone to Watch, AirPods and Vision Pro. The challenge for Ternus is that this machine is already enormous, so growth must come from new categories and new technologies rather than from simply doing more of the same.

What Tim Cook Does Now as Executive Chairman

Cook did not leave Apple. As executive chairman, he is expected to help with selected company matters, and Apple specifically said the role includes engaging with policymakers around the world. That is a meaningful detail, because Apple's business depends heavily on government relationships, from trade and tariffs to privacy rules and app store regulation. Analysts noted that keeping Cook in that role reduces the likelihood of an abrupt break in Apple's government, supply-chain and institutional relationships.

The pay structure was also disclosed. According to one report, Cook will receive a $2 million salary as executive chairman, with a target equity award of $45 million to be granted in fiscal 2027, half of it tied to Apple's stock performance against other S&P 500 companies.

Why Hardware Matters for the AI Era

The choice of a hardware leader is widely read as a strategic signal. Babak Hafezi, a professor of international business at American University, told Al Jazeera that Ternus's appointment is a subtle way of doubling down on hardware innovation as a core strategy, and that it does not refute the Cook era but marks a new stage that interweaves AI with hardware instead of treating AI as a standalone product. Aleksandar Tomic of Boston College argued that focusing on core products could help Apple lead the AI boom over the long run.

That idea fits Apple's long-standing approach. While rivals race to build the biggest models, Apple has tended to focus on devices, custom chips and the user experience, with AI features built into products people already own. If AI becomes a feature inside every phone, laptop and wearable, a company that designs both the silicon and the device has a natural advantage. If instead AI value concentrates in the largest cloud models, Apple could face pressure to partner or catch up.

“ Apple does not need to win the AI race by building the biggest brain. It needs to put the best one in your pocket. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

The Challenges Waiting for Ternus

The new CEO steps in while Apple faces pressure on both the product and operational fronts, as one profile of the new CEO put it. Several challenges stand out.

  • Artificial intelligence. Apple is expected to keep proving that its approach to AI can compete with fast-moving rivals.
  • New product categories. A foldable device and further work on the Vision Pro line are among the areas observers are watching for the next growth chapter.
  • Regulation. App store rules, competition cases and privacy laws in the United States, Europe and Asia continue to shape Apple's services profits.
  • Supply chain and trade. Tariffs and geopolitical tension affect where and how Apple makes its products.
  • Succession depth. Apple has reshuffled its senior ranks, including reported moves such as Johny Srouji taking a chief hardware officer role, and a new leadership bench must prove itself.

The Cook-to-Nvidia Twist

The Apple story took an unexpected turn in November. After Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned, President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that Cook should replace him. Neither Cook nor Apple immediately commented, and there has been no confirmation that Nvidia's board is considering him. Nvidia has appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and said it is searching for a permanent successor, both inside and outside the company.

It is best to treat this as a suggestion and not a plan. Cook is Apple's executive chairman, a role Apple created to keep him engaged with policymakers, and moving to lead a company in a different part of the technology industry would be an enormous step. Still, the suggestion shows how highly Cook's reputation as a steady operator is rated, even by those outside Apple.

Lessons From Apple's Succession for Other Companies

Whatever happens next, the way Apple managed the handover offers a template that other boards can study.

  • Start early. Reports said Cook's successor was widely expected for years, and Ternus was given increasing public visibility long before the announcement.
  • Use a long runway. Months between the announcement and the effective date gave customers, suppliers and investors time to adjust.
  • Keep the former CEO useful. A defined executive chairman role with clear responsibilities, in this case policy engagement, avoids both a power vacuum and a power struggle.
  • Choose strategy, not just a person. The pick of a hardware leader says something about where the company wants to go.
  • Control the message. Careful communication reduces the risk of a market panic.

Apple Compared With a Sudden Exit

It is hard to ignore the contrast with Nvidia's abrupt change at the top. Apple's transition was announced months ahead, rehearsed in public, and supported by a named chairman role. Nvidia's was announced the same day it took effect, after days of reports. Investors tend to reward predictability, and the difference illustrates why governance experts push boards to treat succession as a standing agenda item and not an emergency response.

What to Watch Under Ternus

  • Product launches. Reception of the fall iPhone lineup and any foldable device, and signals about future categories.
  • AI strategy. How Apple weaves AI into its devices and whether it announces new partnerships.
  • Earnings and guidance. Whether growth and margins hold through the first full quarters of the new era.
  • Leadership changes. Further moves on the executive team and any new design or hardware appointments.
  • Regulatory outcomes. Rulings that affect App Store revenue and competition in key markets.
  • Cook's role. Any official update on his duties and any developments tied to the Nvidia suggestion.

The Bigger Picture

Apple's handover is a reminder that great companies are judged on how they renew themselves, not just on how they perform under one leader. The Cook years proved that a supply-chain mastermind could grow a design-led company beyond anyone's expectations. The Ternus years will test whether an engineer can steer the same company through the shift to AI, new device types and tougher regulation.

Product strategy under a new CEO takes time to show up, because Apple's major devices and chips are planned years in advance. That means the first products of the Ternus era reflect decisions made under Cook, and the true imprint of the new leadership will appear gradually. Patience is as important for observers as it is for the company.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is the new CEO of Apple?

John Ternus became Apple's CEO on September 1, 2026. He previously served as senior vice president of hardware engineering and joined Apple in 2001.

Tim Cook is Apple's executive chairman. Apple said the role includes engaging with policymakers around the world and assisting with selected company matters.

How long was Tim Cook the CEO of Apple?

Cook led Apple for fifteen years, from 2011 to 2026, after succeeding Steve Jobs.

Why did Apple choose a hardware executive as CEO?

Analysts say the choice signals a continued focus on hardware and on integrating AI into devices, and it marks a return to a CEO with a product design background.

Will Tim Cook become Nvidia's CEO?

President Trump suggested it publicly, but there is no confirmation that Nvidia's board is considering Cook, and Nvidia has named an interim CEO while it searches for a permanent one.

How did Apple's stock perform under Tim Cook?

According to one report, shares rose more than 2,200 percent during his tenure and the company grew from about $350 billion to about $4.5 trillion in market value. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

John Ternus became Apple's CEO on September 1, 2026, succeeding Tim Cook after fifteen years.

Cook is now executive chairman, with a role that includes engaging with policymakers worldwide.

Ternus is a hardware engineer who joined Apple in 2001, and his pick signals a hardware-plus-AI strategy.

Apple's planned, months-long handover contrasts sharply with Nvidia's sudden CEO exit.

title: Demis Hassabis Steps Down as Google DeepMind CEO: Who Takes Over and What It Means for the AI Race
subtitle: Hassabis becomes chair and Alphabet's chief scientist, Koray Kavukcuoglu takes over operations, and Jeff Dean is reported to be leaving. Here is what it means.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
leaderRole: Chair, Google DeepMind & Chief Scientist, Alphabet
quotes: In AI, the person who leads the research and the person who ships the product are rarely the same, and the best companies learn when to separate those jobs.
In a race this expensive, organizational design is a competitive weapon, and a reshuffle can be a strategy as much as a setback.
Scientific brilliance and operational excellence are different skills.
excerpt: On August 5, 2026, Demis Hassabis stepped down as Google DeepMind CEO to become chair and Alphabet's chief scientist. We explain the changes and what they mean.
content:
AI Leadership Watch 2026

In a single announcement on August 5, 2026, one of the most influential jobs in artificial intelligence changed hands. Demis Hassabis, the Nobel Prize-winning co-founder of DeepMind, stepped down as CEO of Google DeepMind to become the unit's chair and Alphabet's chief scientist. At the same time, Jeff Dean, one of the best-known engineers in Google's history, was reported to be leaving after nearly three decades. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai described the changes as part of a broader reorganization of Google's AI effort. This guide explains who is moving where, why it matters for the AI race, and what business leaders should take from it.

What Google Announced

According to Engadget and other outlets, Hassabis is giving up the CEO title of Google DeepMind but is staying with the company. He becomes chairman of the unit and chief scientist of Alphabet, and he continues to lead Isomorphic Labs, the drug-discovery company spun out of DeepMind's research. Koray Kavukcuoglu, who had been the unit's chief technology officer, becomes a senior vice president reporting directly to Pichai and takes over day-to-day leadership of operations.

Fortune described the change as formalizing a shift that was already under way: a move away from daily management and toward long-term work on artificial general intelligence, often shortened to AGI. Some reports said Hassabis had been stepping back from management for roughly a year, wanting to spend more time on scientific questions. The same set of announcements included the departure of Jeff Dean after about 27 years at Google, which several outlets treated as a sign of how large the reshuffle was.

Pichai had recently pushed back on concerns about Google's AI position after the company posted record results in its cloud division, according to ITPro. The reshuffle arrived against a backdrop of intense competition and reports that Google has lost some top AI employees to rivals including Anthropic and OpenAI in recent months.

“ In AI, the person who leads the research and the person who ships the product are rarely the same, and the best companies learn when to separate those jobs. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

Who Is Demis Hassabis?

Hassabis co-founded DeepMind in London in 2010, building it as a research lab focused on solving intelligence. Google acquired the company in 2014 for a price reported in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Over the years, DeepMind became known for headline results, including systems that mastered complex games and, most importantly, AlphaFold, which predicted the structures of proteins and transformed parts of biology.

In October 2024, Hassabis won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on AlphaFold. In April 2023, Google merged DeepMind with its other major research group, Google Brain, creating Google DeepMind with Hassabis as CEO. That unit now oversees the research behind the Gemini family of AI models and much of the company's AI strategy.

One recurring theme in coverage is that Alphabet is not losing Hassabis but repositioning him. As chief scientist, he can focus on long-horizon research and scientific applications of AI, from drug discovery to materials and energy, while someone else runs the machinery of shipping products to billions of users.

Who Is Koray Kavukcuoglu?

Kavukcuoglu has been one of DeepMind's senior technical leaders and served as chief technology officer of Google DeepMind after the 2023 merger. Under the new structure, he takes charge of day-to-day operations and reports to Pichai. Analysts interpreted his promotion as a signal that Google wants a leader whose main job is to turn research into products, especially around Gemini.

That distinction matters. A research lab and a product organization are measured differently. Researchers are rewarded for breakthroughs that may take years, while product teams are measured on launches, users and revenue each quarter. Google DeepMind has to do both at once, and the reshuffle suggests the company believes the product side now needs the sharpest focus.

Why the Jeff Dean News Matters

Dean joined Google in the late 1990s and became closely associated with many of the company's core technical systems and, later, its AI efforts. His departure after nearly three decades is notable partly because of the symbolism. Dean helped define how Google builds large-scale systems, and his exit follows a period in which a number of senior researchers and engineers have moved among the major AI labs.

Talent mobility is now one of the biggest forces shaping the industry. Top AI researchers are scarce, and the biggest companies compete with enormous compensation packages and promises of computing power. When a leader of Dean's stature leaves, it can influence where other people choose to work and what kind of start-ups appear next. Public details about his plans were limited in early coverage, so readers should watch for updates.

The Bigger Context: The AI Talent and Product War

The shake-up did not happen in isolation. Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are competing across models, enterprise customers, consumer apps and computing capacity. Alphabet has real strengths: custom chips, a huge cloud business, vast distribution through Search, Android and Workspace, and deep research talent. Yet reports about departures to rivals suggested that being a giant is not enough on its own.

That environment is also reshaping capital markets. Anthropic is preparing for a Nasdaq listing, and Google is one of its largest shareholders and a supplier of chips to it, a relationship that shows how competitors and partners can overlap in this industry. For Alphabet, that means it is both competing with the model builders and profiting from their growth, a position that makes its own AI organization especially important to get right.

“ In a race this expensive, organizational design is a competitive weapon, and a reshuffle can be a strategy as much as a setback. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

How to Read This: Two Competing Interpretations

Reasonable observers read the news in different ways, and both are worth hearing.

  • The strategic-focus reading. Google is deliberately separating long-term science from short-term product delivery. Hassabis gets to pursue AGI and scientific discovery, Kavukcuoglu gets a clear product mandate, and the structure fits a more mature phase of the AI market.
  • The pressure reading. Departures to rivals, intense competition and a broad leadership shuffle suggest Google is responding to pressure and needs to move faster on products. In this view, the change is a course correction.

The truth may include elements of both. Companies often frame structural changes as strategy, and sometimes they are, even when pressure is also present. What matters is what the organization delivers over the next several quarters.

What This Means for Business Leaders and Investors

For companies that rely on Google's AI products, including the Gemini models and Google Cloud, the practical question is continuity. Nothing in the announcements suggests a change in the product roadmap, and Hassabis and Kavukcuoglu both remain inside the company, but customers should follow Google's communications for any updates on priorities, pricing and support.

For investors, the key signals will be Alphabet's earnings, its cloud growth and the pace of new Gemini releases. For employees across the technology industry, the story is a reminder that the market for AI talent is fluid and that organizational structure, mission clarity and access to computing power matter as much as pay.

For leaders in any industry, the lesson is that scientific brilliance and operational excellence are different skills. Founders and chief scientists often thrive when they are freed from managing thousands of people, and operators thrive when they have a clear mandate. Knowing when to split those roles is one of the most valuable decisions a board can make.

What to Watch Next

  • Gemini releases. The pace and quality of new models under Kavukcuoglu's day-to-day leadership.
  • Further departures or hires. Whether more senior researchers leave, and where they go.
  • Jeff Dean's next move. Any announcement about his plans after leaving Google.
  • Hassabis's research agenda. New work on AGI, science and Isomorphic Labs.
  • Cloud and earnings data. Whether Google Cloud's growth continues and how AI revenue develops.
  • Competitor moves. Anthropic's public listing and OpenAI's strategy will shape the competitive picture.

Lessons for Founders Who Sell Their Companies

Hassabis's path also offers a case study for founders whose companies are acquired. Many founders leave soon after an acquisition. Hassabis stayed for twelve years, kept scientific independence for much of that time, and eventually moved into a role that fits his strengths. The result is an unusual long-term partnership between a large company and a research founder.

The takeaway for acquirers is that integration works best when it protects what made the company valuable in the first place, while still connecting it to the parent's resources and customers. The takeaway for founders is to think carefully about what role they want in the long run, because the one that makes sense in year one may not fit in year twelve.

The Bigger Picture

Leadership changes in AI labs are not just corporate news. They are signals about how the technology's future may unfold. A company that places its most famous scientist in a chief scientist role while promoting an operations-focused leader to run daily work is making a statement about priorities: build better products faster, and keep the long-term science alive.

Whether that approach works will be visible in product quality and customer adoption over the next year. For now, the best summary is that this was a significant reorganization, not a departure from the field, and that its effects will unfold gradually.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Demis Hassabis leaving Google?

No. He stepped down as CEO of Google DeepMind but remains at the company as chair of the unit and chief scientist of Alphabet, and he continues to lead Isomorphic Labs.

Who replaced Demis Hassabis at Google DeepMind?

Koray Kavukcuoglu, previously the unit's chief technology officer, takes over day-to-day leadership as a senior vice president reporting to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai.

When was the DeepMind leadership change announced?

Alphabet announced the changes on August 5, 2026.

Is Jeff Dean leaving Google?

Several outlets reported that Jeff Dean is leaving Google after about 27 years as part of the same set of leadership changes.

Why did Hassabis step down as CEO?

Coverage says the move formalizes a shift away from daily management toward long-term work on artificial general intelligence and science. Some reports said he had been stepping back for about a year.

Will this change Google's Gemini AI products?

No product changes were announced alongside the news. Observers will watch the pace of Gemini releases under the new structure.

Key Takeaways • DeepMind Shake-Up

Demis Hassabis stepped down as Google DeepMind CEO on August 5, 2026, becoming chair and Alphabet's chief scientist.

Koray Kavukcuoglu now runs day-to-day operations and reports directly to Sundar Pichai.

Jeff Dean was reported to be leaving after nearly three decades at Google.

The change splits long-term science from product delivery in the middle of an intense AI talent race.

In a race this expensive, organizational design is a competitive weapon.

title: Boomerang Founders: Why Aneel Bhusri Returned to Workday and Studied the Steve Jobs Playbook
subtitle: Workday's co-founder came back as CEO in February 2026 and is rebuilding the company like a start-up. Here is why founders return and whether it works.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
quotes: Professional managers are brilliant at optimizing what exists. Founders are sometimes needed to decide what should exist next.
When the ground shifts under a company, the people who built the first foundation are sometimes the only ones who remember how.
A returning founder is one way for a company to try to rediscover urgency.
excerpt: Workday co-founder Aneel Bhusri returned as CEO on February 9, 2026, inspired by Steve Jobs's Apple comeback. We explain the boomerang founder trend and its risks.
content:
Leadership Trend 2026

There is a new pattern in corporate leadership, and it has a nickname: the boomerang founder. These are entrepreneurs who built a company, handed the CEO job to a professional operator, and then came back when the business faced a threat that only a founder seemed able to fix. The clearest 2026 example is Aneel Bhusri, who co-founded Workday in 2005 and returned as CEO on February 9, 2026, effective immediately. In October, he told Fortune that he had studied Steve Jobs's comeback at Apple before his restart. This guide explains who is coming back, why, what the playbook looks like, and what it means for employees, investors and anyone building a company in the age of AI.

What Happened at Workday

Bhusri co-founded Workday with his mentor Dave Duffield in 2005 and ran it for many years. In early 2024 he handed the CEO role to co-CEO Carl Eschenbach and stayed on as executive chair, focusing on product and technology. At the time, he felt his work securing the company's future was complete, according to Fortune's CEO Daily.

Then the environment shifted. On February 9, 2026, Workday announced that Eschenbach was stepping down and Bhusri was returning as CEO immediately. Fortune noted that these were not ordinary times: the rise of AI agents was reshaping enterprise software, and investors were questioning how traditional software-as-a-service companies would fare. One industry analysis, from SaaStr, said Bhusri did not especially want to return, but that the pressure on software companies made it hard to say no, and reported that his stake had lost around $1.3 billion in paper value in less than two years.

In an interview, Bhusri said he came back to help Workday lead again during what he called the biggest technology transformation of our lives, and that he wanted to return the company to a start-up orientation and a growth mindset.

“ Professional managers are brilliant at optimizing what exists. Founders are sometimes needed to decide what should exist next. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

The Steve Jobs Playbook Bhusri Studied

Jobs is the most famous boomerang founder in business history. He was pushed out of Apple in 1985 and returned in 1997 to a company in what Fortune described as a death spiral, so close to bankruptcy that it accepted a $150 million investment from rival Microsoft. During his second act, Apple became one of the most innovative and successful product companies in the world and launched the iPhone.

Bhusri told Fortune that he studied this return extensively before his own restart, so intensely that, by his own account, he drove his management team crazy by sending them Instagram clips of Jobs. His biggest takeaway came from an interview in which Jobs described his ambition to make Apple the biggest start-up in the world. For Jobs, that meant restoring a culture of ownership, accountability, speed and focus, and slashing a sprawling product line down to the few products that mattered most.

Bhusri said Jobs was not just a product genius but a management genius, in the way he organized Apple for success, and that he is trying to bring the same mentality of recreating a start-up mindset with clear accountability.

What Bhusri Has Done Since Returning

Based on interviews and coverage, several concrete moves stand out.

  • A re-founding strategy. Bhusri frames Workday's current phase as a re-founding moment, often called Chapter 4, built around AI agents. He has said that with AI, the company is essentially a start-up again.
  • Fewer, owned AI projects. Fortune reported that, inspired by Jobs's cuts to Apple's product line, Bhusri reduced the number of AI agents in development from 50 to 20 and gave each AI effort a single owner.
  • Headcount cuts. Workday cut about 2.5 percent of its workforce. Bhusri insisted the decision was not driven by cost-cutting or by AI replacing people, and said it was painful, adding that affected employees were offered individual contributor roles.
  • New AI leadership. Workday named Joel Hellermark, founder of recently acquired Sana, as chief AI officer.

Why Boomerang Founders Are Having a Moment

The SaaStr analysis described a classic pattern: a B2B company grows from nothing to a billion dollars in revenue, goes public, hires an experienced operator from a large technology company, and the founder slides into an executive chair role to focus on vision and product. It works well when conditions are stable. It works less well when a technology shift threatens the business model itself.

The argument for bringing founders back is that they have authority, speed and conviction that hired executives may lack. A founder can make a bold call without needing to build consensus from scratch, and employees often listen differently to the person who started the company. Professional operators tend to be optimizers, strong at improving existing systems, while a reinvention may call for someone willing to bet the company on something new.

The same analysis pointed to other examples, including UiPath's founder Daniel Dines returning to lead, and described the broader theme as software founders coming back as AI threatens to reshape the industry. The trend is not limited to software, but AI-driven disruption makes it especially visible there.

“ When the ground shifts under a company, the people who built the first foundation are sometimes the only ones who remember how. — The Empire Insight Editorial Board

The Risks: Why Comebacks Often Fail

For every Jobs, there are founders whose returns did not work out. A comeback carries clear risks, and a good board will weigh them before asking a founder to return.

  • Time and patience. Even Jobs's success took years to build. The SaaStr analysis noted that his best-known results arrived long after his return, and not every company has that runway.
  • Old habits. A founder may revert to the style that worked at an earlier, smaller scale, which can clash with a larger organization.
  • Morale and retention. Restructuring, such as headcount cuts, can hurt trust, even when the leader says the goal is focus and not savings.
  • Succession confusion. A founder's return can signal that the previous CEO was a mistake, which complicates the question of who leads next.
  • Dependence on one person. Putting the company's future in one founder's hands raises the same key-person risk that other companies are facing this month.

The AI and Jobs Question

Bhusri has been unusually direct about how AI could change work. In an interview with Fortune, he said AI will displace a lot of jobs within five years. In another interview he said he worries about college graduates finding work, since many entry-level jobs are the kind that AI could do, and that this is a problem society must solve.

That candor matters because Workday sells software for human resources and finance, the very systems companies use to manage their people and money. If AI agents begin doing more of the work that employees once did, the products used to manage those employees must change as well. Bhusri's view is that customers in HR and finance want a careful, controlled path to AI adoption and not a reckless one, which is the pitch Workday is making.

How This Connects to Other CEO Stories This Month

The boomerang trend sits next to a wave of other leadership stories. Apple completed a planned handover from Tim Cook to John Ternus. Google DeepMind's founder moved from CEO to chair and chief scientist. Nvidia's co-founder resigned abruptly, leaving an interim CEO in charge. Together they show a corporate world in which leadership transitions are being tested harder than usual, largely because AI is forcing every business to rethink what it does and who should lead it.

One way to see the difference is by type. Apple's was an orderly succession. DeepMind's was a role redesign that keeps the founder close. Nvidia's was a sudden exit. Workday's is a founder return. Each solves a different problem, and each shows that there is no single correct way to hand over power.

Lessons for Founders, Boards and Employees

  • Founders: Stepping back is not necessarily permanent. If you stay close as chair, you keep the option to return, and you keep the knowledge needed to do it well.
  • Boards: Define in advance what would trigger a founder's return and how a comeback would be structured, rather than improvising in a crisis.
  • CEOs: Hired operators should expect that a technology shift can change the job description overnight. Strategy documents should plan for disruption, not just optimization.
  • Employees: A founder's return usually brings faster decisions and more change. Clear communication and clear ownership of projects are the best signs the plan is working.
  • Investors: Treat a comeback as a strategic bet, not a guarantee. Look for specific milestones such as product focus, margins and customer retention.

What to Watch at Workday

  • AI agent launches. Whether the smaller set of agents reaches customers quickly and shows real adoption.
  • Financial results. Growth, margins and customer retention over the next several quarters.
  • Talent signals. Hiring, departures and how employees describe the culture shift.
  • Competitive moves. How larger software rivals and AI-native start-ups respond.
  • Leadership bench. Who emerges as Bhusri's long-term successor and what role Duffield continues to play.

The Bigger Picture

The boomerang founder is more than a fashionable story. It reflects a deeper truth about how companies age. Organizations tend to become better at repeating success and worse at changing direction, and a sudden technology shift can expose that weakness. A returning founder is one way for a company to try to rediscover urgency.

Whether the trend will deliver depends on execution, not on nostalgia. Jobs's second act worked because he combined authority with a clear strategy and a few great products. Bhusri is betting that a similar blend of focus, ownership and speed can reposition Workday for the AI era. The answer will arrive in product results and customer numbers, not in interviews. This article is for information only and is not investment advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a boomerang founder?

A boomerang founder is an entrepreneur who steps away from the CEO role, often handing it to a professional manager, and later returns to lead the company again, usually during a period of disruption.

When did Aneel Bhusri return as Workday CEO?

Workday announced on February 9, 2026, that Carl Eschenbach was stepping down and Bhusri was returning as CEO, effective immediately.

What did Aneel Bhusri learn from Steve Jobs?

He said he studied Jobs's return to Apple and took away the importance of restoring a start-up culture of ownership, accountability, speed and focus, including cutting the number of projects to those that matter most.

Did Workday lay off employees?

Workday cut about 2.5 percent of its workforce, according to coverage of Bhusri's remarks. He said the decision was not driven by cost-cutting or by AI replacing people.

Why do founders return to their companies?

Analysts say founders return when a company faces an existential or strategic threat that calls for fast, high-conviction decisions, such as the shift to AI agents in enterprise software.

Do founder comebacks usually succeed?

Results vary. Steve Jobs's return to Apple is the most famous success, but it took years, and many comebacks do not match it. Outcomes depend on strategy, timing and execution.

Key Takeaways • Boomerang Founders

Aneel Bhusri returned as Workday CEO on February 9, 2026, after handing the job to Carl Eschenbach in 2024.

He studied Steve Jobs's Apple comeback and aims to run Workday like a start-up again.

He cut AI agents in development from 50 to 20, gave each a single owner and trimmed 2.5 percent of staff.

Founders return when disruption demands speed and conviction, but comebacks carry real risks.

Managers optimize what exists. Founders sometimes decide what should exist next.

Aneel Bhusri

Co-founder & CEO, Workday California, USA
Feb 9 2026 Returned as CEO
2005 Workday Co-founded
50 to 20 AI Agents in Development

Bottom Line: “A founder returns to turn a mature company back into a start-up.”

title: Victoria Ajoku: The UK Fan Maker Giving an Ancient Craft a Bold New Future
subtitle: How the UK Ambassador for Fan Making and founder of Fan The Glory With Tori is reviving a critically endangered heritage craft through mobile workshops across the United Kingdom.
author: The Empire Insight Editorial Board
leaderRole: Master of Arts, Master Fan Maker, Fan Curator & UK Ambassador for Fan Making
quotes: No endangered craft can thrive behind closed doors.
An artisan cannot be separated from the work they make, so come as you are.
Critically endangered crafts must honour the past while staying open to change.
excerpt: When fan making was classed as a critically endangered UK craft in 2017, Victoria Ajoku saw a call to action. Meet the UK Ambassador for Fan Making and her mission to give the hand fan a future through inclusive mobile workshops.
content:
Creative Entrepreneur • UK Heritage Crafts

What happens to a craft when fewer people learn it, fewer people practise it, and a whole generation grows up barely knowing it exists? For fan making in the UK, that moment arrived in 2017. For Victoria Ajoku, it was not a sad statistic but a call to action.

A UK Craft That Was Running Out of Time

In 2017, fan making was classified as a critically endangered craft. Many people would have read that and moved on. Victoria asked herself a different question: how could she use her business to give fan making a future?

Today, Master of Arts, Master Fan Maker and Fan Curator Victoria Ajoku is the UK Ambassador for Fan Making. Her answer is Fan The Glory With Tori, a UK company that teaches, makes, performs and champions the hand fan for a new audience. It rests on skill and cultural heritage, and on a simple belief: an ancient craft can stay meaningful if someone is willing to learn it, teach it and let it evolve.

From Curiosity to Calling

Victoria's story started quietly. In 2012, she began collecting souvenir hand fans while teaching herself to make accessories by hand, jewellery included. It was creative curiosity and a love of sustainable, handmade crafts, nothing more at the time.

Her master's degree in performance and creative research gave that curiosity a direction. She loved working with props on stage and decorating theatre set designs, which taught her to see a fan as both a practical performance tool and an object with real visual and cultural weight. Her West African heritage made it personal too, since she had known African Chieftaincy fans since childhood.

In 2015 she turned professional. She taught, made handmade fans to sell and took bespoke fan commissions, and those early years laid the foundation for everything that followed.

The Timing That Changed Everything

In 2016, the Heritage Crafts organisation in the UK began gathering research on crafts that are viable, endangered or critically endangered. The aim was to shine a light on skills at risk of disappearing and on the people working to protect them. A year later, fan making landed in the red zone as critically endangered.

Victoria felt the craft needed a new lease of life, and a new voice, face and business to carry it into the modern era. She sensed a deep calling to take on that role.

Filling a Gap in the UK Fan-Making Sector

Early in her career, Victoria noticed that two groups were largely missing from fan making: young people and people from ethnic backgrounds. Looking at the centre stage of the UK sector, she could not find anyone who looked and thought the way she did. So she decided to help fill that space herself.

Her background with fans in dance and singing performance brings the craft to life on stage as well as at the workbench. She describes that pairing as rare, and one that only she offers through Fan The Glory With Tori. For Victoria, representation is more than a talking point. It means turning up, lending a positive voice to the sector and showing that fan making has room for anyone who wants to try it.

Fanning the Way to Freedom: Mobile Fan Making Workshops in the UK

Her company slogan, Fanning the Way to Freedom, sums up what she wants for the craft: free of gatekeeping, free to grow and free for anyone to try.

Victoria runs a mobile service, so she brings fan making workshops to people where they are, in community and public settings the craft has rarely reached. Her workshops are inclusive, fun, educational, entertaining and therapeutic, a mix she says she had not seen from any other fan maker or fan-related company in the UK. People of all ages, backgrounds and abilities can try the craft in a welcoming and safe space.

Her reasons are plain. Fan-making events, she says, have long been organised by the same people in the same venues year after year, so the same voices keep getting heard. Over time that pattern has pushed aside the fans of the African continent, among others, and left the impression that the craft belongs to a select few. Fans are made and used on every continent, and Victoria believes no endangered craft can thrive behind closed doors.

Where Heritage Meets Innovation

Victoria keeps tradition alive by pairing heritage with modern craftsmanship. She teaches classes and sells eco-friendly folding hand fans in a range of sizes, balancing the old with the contemporary.

She was also the first fan maker in the UK to bring paper marbling to handmade folding fans. Paper marbling is an endangered craft in its own right, so the result is something genuinely new: the marbled hand fan, one object that carries two threatened traditions.

“No endangered craft can thrive behind closed doors.— Victoria Ajoku

Leading Through Collaboration

Victoria calls herself a sustainable and innovative leader and a humble solopreneur who is open to collaboration. More than half of her work happens in partnership with other leaders, charities, organisations and businesses. Her style balances autonomy, alliance and what she calls “people empowerment.”

She is also the face of her own brand. She runs every workshop and makes the fan accessories herself, which keeps quality and authenticity intact. She is confident that nobody does what she does in quite the same way.

Building a Brand People Remember

Turning a craft into a business meant finding several ways to get in front of people. Performance, from fan dancing to fan singing, helps her stand out, and networking keeps her in the room. She gives talks, runs demonstrations at craft events and attends business gatherings, always with business cards and QR codes in hand. Social media lets her share and archive her work as it happens.

Her calendar runs well ahead of her. Most collaborations are planned a year in advance and backed by extensive research and field work, and coverage in newspapers, magazines and on television has widened her audience further.

Lessons From the Hard Moments

The road has not been easy. In the early years, Victoria faced discrimination that left her on the margins, and finding a place where her skills and her company were welcomed and supported was hard.

That experience taught her to build her own tribe, a circle within the communities where she could be celebrated. Genuine supporters came from it. She now believes no one is ever truly alone, because a support system can simply be redirected. She also learned to gather people to mark her wins, awards, achievements, scholarships and business anniversaries, because the impact an organisation makes deserves to be recognised and applauded.

Her Advice to Makers and Small Business Owners: Come As You Are

In the classroom, Victoria starts with authenticity. An artisan cannot be separated from the work they make, she says, so makers should let their real selves lead their craft. Trouble tends to start when people imitate someone else or copy a single model that worked for another person. No one formula fits everyone, and makers have to believe in their own products and abilities, or nobody else will.

  • Show up, calm and confident. The right connections can pass by unnoticed.
  • Keep learning. Read, research, try other crafts and take classes in your own field from different teachers.
  • Talk to other makers. Fellow artists and craftspeople share experience you cannot get alone.
  • Solve problems to build skill. It also makes winning clients more likely.
  • Be easy to find locally and online. Have a website, a working phone number and a social media presence.

For anyone starting a business without a business qualification, she offers reassurance. Preparation and knowledge are valuable, but she has found that real-life experience of running a business is what you truly need. Her shortest piece of advice? “Come as you are.”

UK Recognition and International Reach

Victoria is proud and thankful for every award and television appearance. Her screen credits include the BBC's The Repair Shop on the Road, Channel 4's Steph's Packed Lunch and Love Your Weekend with Alan Titchmarsh. She has also been featured in Forbes, i News, The Sunday Telegraph, The Elite X and The Executive Lens. Her teaching has taken her abroad, to Spain and to Amsterdam for the Ambacht en Bleed festival.

The Road Ahead for UK Fan Making

Victoria's ambitions as UK Ambassador for Fan Making are broad. She would like to see fan making move into fresh territory such as the beauty industry, ceramics, advertising and industrial sectors. As an educator, she is designing a syllabus that would let learners earn a certificate in fan crafting, so the craft is respected as a profession and not dismissed as a pastime.

Her work as a Fan Curator is growing as well. She has already curated two fan exhibitions in open public spaces, and she enjoys the influence of gallery curation, which lets her share history and perspectives while uplifting a space. Her goal is to bring the right investors on board so Fan The Glory With Tori can grow into a sustainable company.

Digital platforms are part of the plan. Within five to ten years, she expects more makers of handcrafted products to team up with like-minded influencers on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram to market and sell their work to an international audience.

A Guardian of the Craft

Behind every plan is one idea: critically endangered crafts must honour the past while staying open to change. Victoria describes herself as a custodian and guardian of fan making, and she wants it to stay fresh and current so the next generation can carry it forward.

Fan making was once a craft with few makers and fewer champions. Today it has Victoria Ajoku, and a growing community learning that an old craft can still make a lot of positive noise. She is, without doubt, a true overcomer and a passionate businesswoman, persevering to preserve the heritage craft of fan making.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Victoria Ajoku?

Victoria Ajoku is a Master of Arts, Master Fan Maker, Fan Curator and the UK Ambassador for Fan Making. She is the founder of Fan The Glory With Tori.

Why is fan making an endangered craft in the UK?

In 2017, fan making was classified as critically endangered after the Heritage Crafts organisation in the UK began researching which crafts were viable, endangered or critically endangered.

Where can I find fan making workshops in the UK?

Fan The Glory With Tori is a mobile service, so Victoria Ajoku brings inclusive fan making workshops to people where they are. Workshops suit all ages, backgrounds and abilities.

Can I commission a bespoke handmade fan in the UK?

Yes. Victoria Ajoku has made fans to sell and fulfilled bespoke commissions for clients since 2015, and she sells eco-friendly folding hand fans in a range of sizes.

What is a marbled hand fan?

It is a folding hand fan decorated with paper marbling. Victoria Ajoku was the first fan maker in the UK to introduce paper marbling to handmade folding fans.

Does Victoria Ajoku teach outside the UK?

Yes. Her teaching has taken her to Spain and to Amsterdam for the Ambacht en Bleed festival.

Key Takeaways • Victoria Ajoku

Fan making was classed as critically endangered in 2017, and Victoria Ajoku responded by building a UK business to revive it.

She was the first UK fan maker to bring paper marbling to handmade folding fans.

Her mobile workshops make the craft inclusive, fun and open to all ages and abilities.

She is building a certificate syllabus so fan crafting is respected as a profession.

Her advice to every maker: come as you are.

Gaming Watch • November 2026

After two delays and years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI is now just weeks away. Rockstar and Take-Two have kept one date on the calendar since late 2025, and this month is when it finally arrives. Here is what is confirmed, what is still unknown, and how to get ready without falling for scams.

The Date That Matters: November 19, 2026

Rockstar Games set the release for Thursday, November 19, 2026, after moving it from its earlier May 2026 target. Take-Two has repeated the date in its financial updates since, and its leadership has publicly said it is not planning another slip. As of this writing there is no new delay announcement, which is a big deal for a game that has already moved twice.

Platforms: Console First, PC Still Unconfirmed

GTA VI launches on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S only. There is no official PC date. Some reports point to a PC version in early 2027, but Rockstar has not confirmed anything, so treat those dates as rumor. If you only play on PC, plan to wait and ignore any site that claims to sell an early PC key.

Pre-Orders, Pre-Load and Price

  • Pre-orders: Open now on the major console stores, with reported prices of $79.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the Ultimate edition. Prices can vary by region and retailer, so check your own store page.
  • Pre-load: Digital pre-loading is reported to begin on November 12 at local midnight, which lets you download in advance and play the moment the game unlocks.
  • Unlock time: Some outlets report a rolling local-midnight unlock on launch day. Confirm the exact time on your console store before you plan a late night.
  • Campaign first: The single-player story is the focus at launch. No separate release date has been announced for the online mode.

Rockstar Is Also Releasing an Album

Rockstar has said a 34-track official album will arrive on launch day alongside the game, and it has been rolling out merchandise in the weeks before. It is a sign of how big a cultural event this launch is being treated as, closer to a blockbuster film premiere than a normal game release.

“A big launch rewards the patient: pre-load early, buy from official stores, and trust only Rockstar's own announcements.— The Empire Insight Editorial Board

How to Get Ready Before November 19

  1. Free up storage now. Big open-world games need a lot of space, and pre-loads often require extra room for updates. Clear space before November 12.
  2. Pre-load on a wired connection if you can, and start early in the day so any problems show up before launch night.
  3. Check your console version. Only PS5 and Xbox Series X|S are supported, not older consoles.
  4. Stay safe from scams. Expect fake giveaways, leaked-build downloads and cheap “keys”. Buy only from official stores or well-known retailers.
  5. Set expectations for kids. The series is for mature audiences, so set up parental controls if younger players share your console.

What We Still Don't Know

Details that remain unconfirmed in official channels include the exact file size, a PC release date, extra editions beyond those listed, and the shape of the online mode after launch. Anything beyond Rockstar and Take-Two announcements should be read as speculation.

When does GTA 6 come out?

Thursday, November 19, 2026, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

Is GTA 6 coming to PC?

No PC release date has been officially announced. Reports of early 2027 are unconfirmed.

When can I pre-load GTA 6?
